headword: {諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}
gloss: all things are impermanent; nothing lasts forever

definitions.gloss: all things are impermanent; the transience of all phenomena
definitions.explanation: A Buddhist teaching that all conditioned things are in constant flux and nothing remains unchanged. One of the most well-known phrases in Japanese literature and philosophy.

examples.japanese: {諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}、すべて⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧⟦{移|うつ}り{変|か}わる→移り変わる：19543_utsurikawaru⟧。
examples.english: All things are impermanent — everything changes.

examples.japanese: {祇園精舎|ぎおんしょうじゃ}⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{鐘|かね}→鐘：02654_kane⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{声|こえ}→声：02207_koe⟧、{諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{響|ひび}き→響き：00098_hibiki⟧あり。
examples.english: The bells of Gion Monastery echo with the sound of impermanence.
examples.notes: Opening line of The Tale of the Heike.

examples.japanese: {栄華|えいが}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{誇|ほこ}った→誇る：14180_hokoru⟧⟦{城|しろ}→城：03255_shiro⟧⟦も→も：00484_mo⟧⟦{今|いま}→今：00945_ima⟧⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧⟦{廃墟|はいきょ}→廃墟：12453_haikyo⟧となり、{諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{感|かん}じる→感じる：02044_kanjiru⟧。
examples.english: The castle that once boasted of its splendor is now a ruin, making one feel the impermanence of all things.

notes:
One of the Three Marks of Existence in Buddhism, expressing that all conditioned phenomena are transient. This phrase is deeply embedded in Japanese culture and literature.

The most famous use is the opening of {平家物語|へいけものがたり} (The Tale of the Heike): "{祇園精舎|ぎおんしょうじゃ}⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{鐘|かね}→鐘：02654_kane⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{声|こえ}→声：02207_koe⟧、{諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{響|ひび}き→響き：00098_hibiki⟧あり" — a passage that most Japanese people learn in school.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{感|かん}じる→感じる：02044_kanjiru⟧ (to feel the impermanence of things)
- {諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}⟦の→の：09472_no⟧{理|ことわり} (the truth of impermanence)

Often invoked when reflecting on the passage of time, the fall of the powerful, or the fleeting nature of beauty and success.
